title: Traumatic arrest and thoracotomy
stem: Resus 1. A 22-year-old man was stabbed once, just left of the sternum. He lost his radial pulse three minutes ago in the ambulance and CPR is in progress as he comes through the door. A cardiothoracic surgeon is in the building. You lead.

phases.title: Mobilise
phases.goal: The surgeon, the kit, blood and PPE; the time he lost his pulse.

phases.title: Assess
phases.goal: Pulse, ultrasound, pupils: is this salvageable?

phases.title: HOTT
phases.goal: Name it, decide on thoracotomy, and fix the reversible causes at the same time.

phases.title: Clamshell
phases.goal: Open the chest and the pericardium correctly.

phases.title: After ROSC
phases.goal: Where next, and what bleeds once the pressure returns?

review.text: Time window. ERC 2021 and RCUK give about 10–15 minutes from loss of signs of life for penetrating trauma; some US guidance (EAST) allows up to 15 minutes of CPR for penetrating injury. The script says within 15 minutes.

notes:
Checked against the European Resuscitation Council 2021 guidelines (traumatic cardiac arrest), Resuscitation Council UK 2021, and ATLS 11th edition.

Traumatic cardiac arrest is treated by fixing its causes at the same time: HOTT (Hypovolaemia, Oxygenation, Tension pneumothorax, Tamponade). Chest compressions do not take priority over these, because compressing an empty or tamponaded heart achieves little. Adrenaline has a limited role.

Resuscitative thoracotomy (clamshell) in the ED is indicated for penetrating chest trauma with arrest, especially with tamponade, when the time since loss of signs of life is short (ERC: within about 10–15 minutes). Outcomes after blunt trauma arrest are poor. It is done by a trained operator; the station expects you to lead, prepare and understand the steps.

Pericardiocentesis is not the treatment for traumatic tamponade: the blood clots. Open the pericardium.

Clamshell: bilateral 4th/5th intercostal space incisions from the mid-axillary lines meeting across the sternum, sternum divided, retractor, pericardium lifted and opened longitudinally in front of the phrenic nerve, clot evacuated, cardiac wound controlled with a finger (then sutures or a Foley catheter), internal cardiac massage, descending aortic compression if needed. Ligate the internal mammary arteries after ROSC.

Your notes list 'Thoracotomy' as a topic without detail; nothing conflicts.

Perfect script checked against the ERC traumatic arrest algorithm, an ATLS checklist, an HKCEM-style scheme and a keyword scheme. Removed the wrong options (pericardiocentesis, standard ALS only, CT after ROSC). Added: traumatic arrest and HOTT named, the indication for thoracotomy said aloud, why not a needle, blood with calcium and TXA after ROSC, and the handover questions scored.

badge.name: Clamshell
badge.flavor: HOTT, not just CPR. Longitudinal, in front of the phrenic.

cards.q: Reversible causes addressed first in traumatic cardiac arrest?
cards.why: HOTT, treated simultaneously, before or with compressions.

cards.q: Traumatic tamponade in arrest is treated by…
cards.why: Clotted blood needs the pericardium opened.

options: Longitudinal, anterior to the phrenic nerve
Longitudinal, posterior to the phrenic nerve

cards.q: ED thoracotomy outcomes are best for…
options: Blunt trauma with arrest at scene
cards.why: Isolated cardiac stab wounds with tamponade have the best survival.

cards.q: After ROSC from clamshell, which vessels start bleeding?
options: The pulmonary veins at the hilum
cards.why: They were cut with the sternum; tie them.

options: Pericardial fluid with RV diastolic collapse
Pericardial fluid with a hyperdynamic, full RV
Absent lung sliding on one side
cards.why: The pressure collapses the thin-walled right heart in diastole.

script.say: Cardiothoracic surgeon to resus now. Open the thoracotomy set: Gigli saw or heavy shears. Major haemorrhage protocol: blood through the rapid infuser. PPE with eye protection.
When exactly did he lose his pulse? Rhythm on your monitor? The wound?
script.do: Lost his pulse at 21:14, 3 minutes ago; narrow complex about 100; a single 2 cm stab left of the sternum.

script.say: No carotid or femoral pulse; organised complexes: PEA. Subxiphoid ultrasound: fluid around the heart, ventricles barely moving: tamponade. Pupils reactive.
This is a traumatic cardiac arrest: we treat HOTT at the same time, not standard ALS. Hypovolaemia, oxygenation, tension, tamponade.

Penetrating chest wound, signs of life lost 3 minutes ago, tamponade on ultrasound: a resuscitative thoracotomy is indicated, within 15 minutes. No needle pericardiocentesis: traumatic tamponade is clotted blood. We open the pericardium.
Together: blood through the rapid infuser; intubate and ventilate; bilateral finger thoracostomies; and a clamshell thoracotomy for the tamponade.

Clamshell: incisions in both 4th or 5th spaces joined across the sternum, sternum divided, retractor in. Lift the pericardium and open it longitudinally, in front of the phrenic nerve. Clot out, finger on the hole, then sutures or a Foley as a bridge.

Straight to theatre with the cardiothoracic surgeon, not CT. Clamp or tie the internal mammary arteries: they bleed once the pressure returns. Keep the blood going 1:1:1 with calcium; tranexamic acid.
